rows.row: NR-H4 Field Data partner form
rows.before:
For insurers, underwriters and inspectors

If you’re working on condition-based roof underwriting, we want to build the data with you: what to measure, how often and in what format.

  • Pilot: a set of treated roofs with full records, in a market you choose
  • Format: records built around the fields your models need
  • Access: Roof Records shared with the homeowner’s permission

rows.row: NR-H6 Technical data sheet request form
rows.before:
Request data sheets

Technical data sheets, safety data sheets, application protocols and sample warranties.

  • Architects and engineers: spec language and submittals
  • Property managers: documentation for boards and insurers
  • Contractors: application protocols for certified dealers

rows.row: NR-H7 Qualify 5-question self-check funnel
rows.before:
Quick self-check

Five questions from the ground. It isn’t an assessment, but it tells you what to expect from one. Prefer a photo? Try the photo roof check.

Are your shingles asphalt (not metal, tile or wood)?
Is any part of the roof sagging or soft underfoot?
Is there an active leak right now?
Are shingles missing, curling or cracked in many places?
Do you see fading, dark streaks or granules in the gutters?

Answer the questions to see what to expect.

rows.row: NR-H9 Contact routing of form messages (what to send, where it goes)
rows.before:
Have these ready

It helps us route you to the right person the first time.

  • About your roof: the property address and roughly how old the roof is
  • Warranty claim: your warranty number, the address and photos of the problem
  • Portfolio: the number of buildings and where they are
  • Becoming a dealer: your company name, trade and service area

Where your message goes

  • Homeowners: to the certified dealer for your area
  • Warranty claims: to Nano Products LLC and your dealer, in writing
  • Portfolios and commercial: to the team that runs multi-building surveys
  • Contractors: to dealer development

rows.row: NR-C1 bond-energy comparison and the UV inference drawn from it
rows.before:
Why sunlight can’t break it

Asphalt is a hydrocarbon, held together largely by carbon bonds. Ultraviolet light carries enough energy to break them, which is what starts the aging loop on every shingle roof.

Silicone’s backbone is silicon and oxygen, the same pairing as quartz. That bond takes more energy to break than ultraviolet light delivers, so the material stays intact where asphalt breaks down.
